why_use_this:
Reach for this package when you need to find the input that minimizes (or, for `simplex_solve`, maximizes subject to linear constraints) a function -- fitting a model's parameters, finding a system's equilibrium, solving a resource-allocation problem. It covers three genuinely different problem shapes with different tools: unconstrained smooth optimization (gradient descent through Newton's method, picked by how much curvature information you're willing to supply), constrained optimization via the penalty method (turns constraints into an added cost term so an unconstrained solver can still be used), and linear programming via the simplex method (exact, for problems that are genuinely linear in both objective and constraints). If your problem is a nonlinear ROOT-finding problem (\( F(x)=0 \)) rather than a minimization problem, that's [vani-algebra](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-algebra)'s `algebra_newton_system` instead, even though the underlying Newton-step machinery looks similar. Every gradient-consuming function here also has a `_fd` (finite-difference) variant for when you don't have or don't want to hand-derive an analytic gradient/Hessian, and a `_closure` variant (v0.1.5) for when your objective needs to capture data by reference instead of being a plain top-level function pointer.

Many of the unconstrained-solver notes below reuse one running example: minimizing \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\) (the sphere function) starting from \((3,4)\) -- deliberately a 3-4-5 triangle so the numbers stay clean.

sphere_fn.intuition: The simplest possible "bowl" shape: a single minimum at the origin, and it looks exactly the same in every direction you approach it from (its cross-sections are circles, not stretched ellipses) -- the friendliest possible test case for any minimization method, since there's no valley to get lost in and no direction that's harder to descend than another.
sphere_fn.example: At the running example's starting point \((3,4)\): \(f(3,4) = 3^2+4^2 = 9+16=25\).
sphere_fn.why: Used throughout this package's own tests as the "should just work, and work fast" sanity check -- if a solver struggles here, something is genuinely wrong with it; contrast with `rosenbrock_fn` below, deliberately chosen to be hard even for correct solvers.

sphere_grad.intuition: The gradient of a sum of squares is just twice each variable -- makes sense since \(d(x^2)/dx=2x\) for each term independently.
sphere_grad.example: At \((3,4)\): \(\nabla f = 2\times(3,4) = (6,8)\) -- points directly AWAY from the origin, confirming the gradient (direction of steepest INCREASE) points away from the minimum, as it should.
sphere_grad.why: This gradient reappears throughout the other worked examples below (`gradient_descent_fixed`, `armijo_line_search`, `newton_nd`, ...) -- all applied to this same starting point, so you can compare how differently each method handles the identical first step.

rosenbrock_fn.intuition: Shaped like a curved banana-shaped valley: the minimum is easy to get NEAR (the valley itself is easy to find) but hard to get precisely TO, because the valley floor curves and plain gradient descent's straight-line steps keep overshooting across the narrow valley instead of running smoothly along it.
rosenbrock_fn.why: The coefficient \(100\) is what makes this hard -- it makes the valley extremely narrow in one direction and extremely long in the other, so a fixed or naively-chosen step size that works well across the narrow direction takes forever to make progress along the long direction, and vice versa. This is exactly the kind of function where `newton_nd` (which accounts for curvature) dramatically outperforms plain gradient descent.

rosenbrock_grad.intuition: Straightforward calculus applied to `rosenbrock_fn`'s two squared terms -- the chain rule on each.
rosenbrock_grad.example: At \((0,0)\): \(\partial f/\partial x = -2(1-0)-400(0)(0-0) = -2-0=-2\). \(\partial f/\partial y = 200(0-0)=0\). So \(\nabla f(0,0)=(-2,0)\) -- pointing in the \(-x\) direction, i.e. AWAY from the minimum at \((1,1)\) in the \(x\)-coordinate specifically (consistent: increasing \(x\) from 0 initially does reduce \(f\), moving toward \(x=1\)).
rosenbrock_grad.why: Notice the \(y\)-partial is comparatively simple (\(200(y-x^2)\)) while the \(x\)-partial is more tangled (it appears in BOTH squared terms) -- this asymmetry between the two directions is part of why the valley is so much easier to descend along one axis than the other.

grad_fd.intuition: When you don't have (or don't want to derive) an exact formula for the gradient, you can still estimate it directly from the function's own behavior: nudge one variable slightly in each direction and see how much the output changes, the same central-difference idea used throughout this ecosystem for numerical derivatives.
grad_fd.example: Estimate \(\partial f/\partial x\) for `sphere_fn` at \((3,4)\) with \(h=0.01\): \(f(3.01,4) = 3.01^2+16 = 9.0601+16=25.0601\). \(f(2.99,4)=2.99^2+16=8.9401+16=24.9401\). Central difference: \(\dfrac{25.0601-24.9401}{0.02}=\dfrac{0.12}{0.02}=6.0\) -- matching `sphere_grad`'s exact analytic answer of \(6\) at this point precisely.
grad_fd.why: Computing a full \(n\)-dimensional gradient this way costs \(2n\) evaluations of \(f\) (two per variable) -- fine for a handful of variables, but noticeably more expensive than one analytic gradient evaluation once \(n\) grows large.

hessian_fd.intuition: The same nudge-and-measure idea as `grad_fd`, one derivative order up -- estimating how the SLOPE itself changes, which needs comparing function values across a small grid of nudges rather than just along each axis individually.
hessian_fd.formula: A finite-difference second-derivative stencil applied to every pair of directions, \(O(n^2)\) evaluations of \(f\) total.
hessian_fd.example: For `sphere_fn`, the true Hessian is the constant matrix \(2I\) (every diagonal entry \(2\), every off-diagonal entry \(0\)) everywhere -- `hessian_fd` at any point should recover something very close to \(\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}\), with only the small finite-difference error the README quantifies (roughly \(10^{-6}\) to \(10^{-4}\), depending on \(h\)) distinguishing it from the exact answer.
hessian_fd.why: \(O(n^2)\) function evaluations for the Hessian (versus \(O(n)\) for the gradient) is a real cost that grows fast -- for a problem with many variables, `newton_nd_fd` becomes noticeably more expensive per step than `newton_nd` with an analytic Hessian, on top of being less accurate.

gradient_descent_fixed.intuition: The most direct possible strategy: figure out which way is downhill (the negative gradient), take a step of some fixed size in that direction, repeat. No cleverness about HOW big a step to take -- that's entirely up to whatever value you pass in.
gradient_descent_fixed.example: Starting the running example at \((3,4)\) with a fixed step size \(\alpha=0.1\): \(\nabla f(3,4)=(6,8)\) (from `sphere_grad`). New point: \((3,4) - 0.1\times(6,8) = (3-0.6,\ 4-0.8) = (2.4,\,3.2)\). Check progress: \(f(2.4,3.2)=5.76+10.24=16\), down from \(f(3,4)=25\) -- real progress, but notice it took one whole step to reduce the value by only \(9\) out of \(25\); reaching the origin exactly would take many more steps at this fixed size.
gradient_descent_fixed.why: The step size \(\alpha\) is entirely the caller's responsibility here -- too large (try \(\alpha=1\) on this same example: you'd land at \((3-6,4-8)=(-3,-4)\), where \(f=25\) again, NO progress at all, having overshot straight past the minimum) and the method can fail to converge or even diverge; too small and it converges correctly but painfully slowly. `armijo_line_search`/`gradient_descent_backtracking` exist specifically to remove this guesswork.

armijo_line_search.intuition: Rather than committing to a step size in advance, try the biggest reasonable step first (\(\alpha=1\)), and check whether it actually reduced the function enough to be worth it; if not, try half as big, then half again, until one finally passes the test.
armijo_line_search.formula: Backtrack \(\alpha\) from \(1\) (halving each rejection) until \(f(x+\alpha d) \le f(x) + c_1\alpha\nabla f(x)^Td\).
armijo_line_search.example: From \((3,4)\), descent direction \(d=-\nabla f=(-6,-8)\), using \(c_1=0.1\). Try \(\alpha=1\) first: new point \((3,4)+(-6,-8)=(-3,-4)\), \(f(-3,-4)=9+16=25\) -- NO better than \(f(3,4)=25\) (this is `gradient_descent_fixed`'s overshoot example from above). Check the Armijo condition: \(\nabla f^Td = (6,8)\cdot(-6,-8)=-36-64=-100\); required threshold is \(25+0.1\times1\times(-100)=25-10=15\); actual value \(25\) is NOT \(\le15\), so \(\alpha=1\) is REJECTED. Halve: try \(\alpha=0.5\): new point \((3,4)+0.5(-6,-8)=(0,0)\), \(f(0,0)=0\); threshold is \(25+0.1\times0.5\times(-100)=25-5=20\); \(0\le20\) -- ACCEPTED. So \(\alpha=0.5\) is chosen, and (for this particular symmetric example) it happens to land EXACTLY on the true minimum in one step.
armijo_line_search.why: This is the mechanism that saves `gradient_descent_fixed`'s overshoot failure above -- rather than blindly taking the full step and landing back at \(f=25\), backtracking catches the failure and retries smaller until it finds a step that provably helps.

gradient_descent_backtracking.intuition: Plain gradient descent, but re-running `armijo_line_search` fresh at every single iteration instead of trusting one fixed step size to stay good for the whole run.
gradient_descent_backtracking.formula: \[ x_{k+1} = x_k - \alpha_k\nabla f(x_k) \] with \(\alpha_k\) chosen fresh each iteration via `armijo_line_search`.
gradient_descent_backtracking.example: Reusing `armijo_line_search`'s example directly: starting from \((3,4)\), the first (and in this case only necessary) iteration already finds \(\alpha_0=0.5\) and lands at \((0,0)\), the exact minimum -- for this particular symmetric sphere-function example, backtracking gradient descent converges in a single step, something `gradient_descent_fixed` with a naive \(\alpha=0.1\) would need many more steps to match.
gradient_descent_backtracking.why: The cost of re-running a line search every iteration is extra function evaluations per step (each halving attempt costs one more evaluation of \(f\)) -- more expensive per iteration than a fixed step size, but far more robust: it can never take a step that provably makes things worse.

newton_nd.intuition: Gradient descent only knows which way is downhill; Newton's method also knows how QUICKLY the slope itself is changing (the curvature, via the Hessian), so it can jump much more directly toward the minimum instead of taking many small downhill steps.
newton_nd.example: For `sphere_fn` at \((3,4)\): the Hessian is the constant \(H=2I=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}\), so \(H^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0\\0&0.5\end{pmatrix}\). Newton step: \((3,4) - H^{-1}(6,8) = (3,4) - (0.5\times6,\ 0.5\times8) = (3-3,\,4-4)=(0,0)\) -- the EXACT minimum, in a single step.
newton_nd.why: This isn't a coincidence for this particular example -- Newton's method is EXACT in one step for any purely quadratic function (like `sphere_fn`), since the method's whole derivation assumes the function looks quadratic near the current point, and here it's quadratic EVERYWHERE, not just nearby. For `rosenbrock_fn` (genuinely non-quadratic), Newton's method would still converge much faster than gradient descent, but wouldn't finish in a single step.

newton_nd_fd.intuition: The same Newton's-method idea as `newton_nd`, but plugging in `hessian_fd`'s estimated Hessian instead of requiring an exact analytic one -- for whenever hand-deriving second derivatives is impractical.
newton_nd_fd.formula: Same update as `newton_nd`, with \(H\) approximated via `hessian_fd`.
newton_nd_fd.example: For `sphere_fn` at \((3,4)\), `hessian_fd` returns something extremely close to the exact \(2I\) (see `hessian_fd`'s own example) -- so this variant's step lands extremely close to \((0,0)\) too, off by only the small finite-difference error, not qualitatively different from the exact-Hessian result here.
newton_nd_fd.why: The gap between `newton_nd` and `newton_nd_fd` only really shows up on a function whose true Hessian VARIES across the domain (unlike `sphere_fn`'s constant one) -- there, the finite-difference estimate is only a LOCAL approximation valid near the current point, whereas an analytic Hessian is exact everywhere it's evaluated.

coordinate_descent.intuition: Instead of moving in the full gradient direction (which requires knowing the gradient at all), fix every variable except one, find the best value for that ONE variable via a simple 1D search, then move to the next variable and repeat -- like solving a Rubik's cube one face at a time instead of trying to plan every move at once.
coordinate_descent.formula: Cycle through \(i=1,\ldots,n\), minimizing along \(x_i\) alone with every other coordinate held fixed, via a 1D line search.
coordinate_descent.example: For `sphere_fn` starting at \((3,4)\): first minimize over \(x\) alone with \(y=4\) fixed: \(f(x,4)=x^2+16\), minimized at \(x=0\) (giving \(f=16\)) -- move to \((0,4)\). Then minimize over \(y\) alone with \(x=0\) fixed: \(f(0,y)=y^2\), minimized at \(y=0\) -- move to \((0,0)\). After one full cycle through both coordinates, already at the exact minimum \((0,0)\).
coordinate_descent.why: `sphere_fn` is a special case where the two variables don't interact at all in the formula (no cross term like \(xy\)), which is exactly why coordinate descent converges so fast here -- for a function where the variables genuinely interact (like `rosenbrock_fn`'s \(100(y-x^2)^2\) term, which tangles \(x\) and \(y\) together), coordinate descent would need many more cycles, since improving one coordinate can "un-optimize" the other.

quadratic_minimize.intuition: For the special case of a quadratic objective, calculus gives an EXACT formula for the minimum directly -- no iteration needed at all, just solve one linear system.
quadratic_minimize.formula: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^TQx-b^Tx\): setting \(\nabla f(x)=Qx-b=0\) gives \(x^*=Q^{-1}b\) (via `mat_solve`, not explicit inversion).
quadratic_minimize.example: Let \(Q=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}\), \(b=(4,6)\). Solve \(Qx^*=b\): \(2x^*_1=4\Rightarrow x^*_1=2\); \(2x^*_2=6\Rightarrow x^*_2=3\). So \(x^*=(2,3)\) -- the exact minimizer, found in one linear solve, no iteration.
quadratic_minimize.why: This is only possible because the problem is EXACTLY quadratic -- for `rosenbrock_fn` or any other genuinely nonlinear objective, there's no such direct formula, which is exactly why the iterative methods above (gradient descent, Newton's method) exist at all.

steepest_descent_quadratic.intuition: Ordinary gradient descent needs the caller to guess or search for a good step size; for a QUADRATIC objective specifically, calculus gives you the mathematically optimal step size directly, in closed form, so no guessing or line search is needed.
steepest_descent_quadratic.example: Using `quadratic_minimize`'s same \(Q=2I\), \(b=(4,6)\), starting from \(x_0=(0,0)\): \(\nabla f(x_0)=Qx_0-b=-b=(-4,-6)\). \(g^Tg = 16+36=52\). \(Qg = (2\times-4,\,2\times-6)=(-8,-12)\). \(g^TQg = (-4)(-8)+(-6)(-12)=32+72=104\). \(\alpha_0=52/104=0.5\). New point: \(x_1 = x_0-\alpha_0g = (0,0)-0.5(-4,-6)=(2,3)\) -- exactly \(x^*\) from `quadratic_minimize`'s example, in a single step.
steepest_descent_quadratic.why: Converging in one step here is a special property of \(Q\) being a multiple of the identity matrix (an "isotropic" quadratic, equally curved in every direction) -- for a more general \(Q\) with different curvature in different directions, steepest descent would still use this same optimal-step-size formula each iteration, but would typically need MANY iterations, zig-zagging back and forth across the narrow direction of the bowl (the same qualitative struggle `rosenbrock_fn` causes plain gradient descent).

penalty_value.intuition: Turn a constraint into a cost: as long as you're on the ALLOWED side of the constraint, add nothing extra to the objective; the moment you cross into FORBIDDEN territory, add a penalty that grows the further you go -- so an unconstrained solver, just trying to minimize the combined total, gets steered away from violating the constraint without needing any special constraint-handling logic of its own.
penalty_value.example: Minimize \(f(x)=x^2\) subject to \(x\ge1\) (written as \(g(x)=1-x\le0\)), with penalty weight \(\mu=10\). At \(x=0\) (violates the constraint, since \(g(0)=1>0\)): penalty term \(=10\times\max(0,1)^2=10\). Combined value: \(f(0)+10 = 0+10=10\). At \(x=1\) (exactly satisfies the constraint, \(g(1)=0\)): penalty \(=10\times\max(0,0)^2=0\). Combined value: \(f(1)+0=1\).
penalty_value.why: Notice the combined objective STRONGLY prefers \(x=1\) (value \(1\)) over \(x=0\) (value \(10\)), even though \(x=0\) is where the UNCONSTRAINED \(f(x)=x^2\) alone would want to be -- the penalty term is doing its job, pulling the minimizer of the COMBINED objective toward the feasible region.

penalty_method_minimize.intuition: A single penalty weight \(\mu\) is always a compromise -- too small and constraint violations aren't punished enough to matter; too large and the combined objective becomes numerically difficult ("ill-conditioned") for an unconstrained solver to handle well. The fix: start with a small, easy-to-optimize \(\mu\), solve, then increase \(\mu\) and re-solve starting from the PREVIOUS answer, repeating until the constraint is satisfied closely enough.
penalty_method_minimize.formula: Minimize `penalty_value`'s combined objective, increase \(\mu\), re-minimize from the previous solution, repeat.
penalty_method_minimize.example: Continuing `penalty_value`'s example (\(f(x)=x^2\), constraint \(x\ge1\)): for a given \(\mu\), the unconstrained minimizer of \(x^2+\mu(1-x)^2\) (found by setting the derivative to zero: \(2x-2\mu(1-x)=0 \Rightarrow x=\mu/(1+\mu)\)) is \(x=\mu/(1+\mu)\). At \(\mu=10\): \(x=10/11\approx0.909\) -- close to the true constrained answer \(x=1\), but not quite there, still slightly on the wrong side. At \(\mu=100\): \(x=100/101\approx0.990\) -- noticeably closer. As \(\mu\to\infty\), \(x\to1\) exactly, the true constrained minimum.
penalty_method_minimize.why: This sequence -- \(0.909\), then \(0.990\), converging toward \(1\) -- is the penalty method's whole story in miniature: each fixed \(\mu\) only gets you APPROXIMATELY to the constrained answer, with the approximation improving as \(\mu\) grows, which is exactly why the algorithm re-solves at a sequence of increasing \(\mu\) values instead of picking one \(\mu\) and stopping.

simplex_solve.intuition: For a problem that's linear in both what you're optimizing and the constraints you must obey, the optimal answer is ALWAYS at a corner (vertex) of the feasible region -- never in the middle of an edge or face. The simplex method exploits this by walking from corner to corner along the region's edges, always moving to a neighboring corner that improves the objective, until no such improving move exists.
simplex_solve.formula: Maximize \(c^Tx\) subject to \(Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\), by pivoting between basic feasible solutions (vertices).
simplex_solve.example: Maximize \(3x_1+2x_2\) subject to \(x_1+x_2\le4\), \(x_1\le2\), \(x_1,x_2\ge0\). The feasible region's corners are \((0,0)\), \((2,0)\), \((2,2)\) (from \(x_1=2\) combined with \(x_1+x_2=4\)), and \((0,4)\). Evaluate the objective at each: \((0,0)\to0\); \((2,0)\to6\); \((2,2)\to3(2)+2(2)=6+4=10\); \((0,4)\to2(4)=8\). The best corner is \((2,2)\), giving \(10\) -- and this is exactly the corner `simplex_solve` would walk to, without needing to check every corner by brute force the way this by-hand example just did.
simplex_solve.why: Checking every corner by hand (as the example does) works fine for a small problem with 2 variables and a handful of corners, but the number of corners can grow explosively with more variables and constraints -- the simplex method's real value is reaching the best corner by a sequence of LOCAL improving moves, never needing to enumerate every corner explicitly.

simplex_value.intuition: Once you have a candidate point (typically the vertex `simplex_solve` found), this just plugs it into the linear objective directly.
simplex_value.example: Using `simplex_solve`'s example, objective \(c=(3,2)\) at the optimal point \((2,2)\): \(3\times2+2\times2=6+4=10\) -- matching the value already identified as the maximum.
simplex_value.why: A small but useful separation of concerns: `simplex_solve` finds WHERE the optimum is, `simplex_value` answers WHAT the objective is worth there -- useful for checking a candidate solution's value without re-running the whole solve, e.g. when comparing several candidate corners by hand the way `simplex_solve`'s example does.
